title: INTERIM ORDER BY SUPREME COURT
content:
Supreme Court has issued an interim order on a writ petition filed against the trend of taking action against students for speaking Nepali in private schools.

Law students Ayush Badal, Smriti Adhikari, and Vivek Bakhrel had filed a writ petition alleging that students were being beaten and fined for speaking Nepali in private schools, arguing that such practices were unconstitutional.

Supreme Court has also issued an interim order and a show cause order in the name of the opposition.

title: PLANNING TO OBSTRUCT TODAY'S PARLIAMENT
content:
Nepal's politics witnessed fresh turmoil as opposition parties demanded the resignation of Home Minister Ramesh Lekhak over a visit visa scandal. The controversy involved alleged misuse and irregularities in how visit visas were being issued.

Although there was no clear evidence proving Minister Lekhak’s direct involvement, the opposition argued that he should have stepped down to allow a fair and transparent investigation. They believed his position could have influenced the inquiry process.

His party, Nepali Congress, defended him, saying he was not involved in any wrongdoing and that the resignation calls were politically motivated.

Despite this, pressure from opposition parties continued to grow. Major groups like the CPN (Maoist Centre) and Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) warned they would block Tuesday’s parliamentary session if Lekhak did not resign.

A leader from the CPN (Maoist Centre) had stated, “We want accountability from those in power. The Home Minister should take responsibility.”

This situation created significant tension in the political arena. With both sides refusing to back down, the parliamentary session faced disruptions and strong debates. The country closely watched as the political drama unfolded.

title: EX HUSBAND KILLED EX WIFE & DAUGHTER
content:
Three members of the same family were murdered in Butwal. A woman and her two daughters were brutally killed at Horizon Chowk. The victims were Deepa Basyal, about 34 years old, and her daughters, seven-year-old Sneha and four-year-old Himani.
According to the police, the main suspect is Deepa’s ex-husband, Sujan Koirala. The couple had divorced a few years ago. Sujan had previously been jailed for killing his own brother but was reportedly pardoned. Police believe he called Deepa to the house and then killed her and their daughters.

title: WAIT WHAT?? HIGH COURT ACQUITTED ALAM
content:
Birgunj bench of the High Court has acquitted former Nepali Congress lawmaker Mohammad Aftab Alam in a high-profile murder case linked to a deadly bomb explosion and killing in Rautahat district.

Alam had earlier been convicted by the Rautahat District Court and sentenced to life imprisonment for his alleged role in the murder of a person by burning him alive in a brick kiln in Rajpur, Rautahat. The incident occurred on the night before the Constituent Assembly elections on 27 Chaitra 2064.

According to the District Court’s ruling, Alam was involved in detonating a bomb that injured several people. To hide evidence, it was alleged that he arranged for the injured individuals to be burned in a brick kiln. The case remained dormant for over a decade until Rautahat police arrested Alam on 19 Asoj 2076 — nearly 12 years after the incident.

The High Court, however, overturned the earlier verdict, citing lack of sufficient evidence to uphold the conviction. This acquittal has triggered varied responses across the political spectrum, with some calling for deeper scrutiny into the case, while others claim the court has rectified an unjust ruling.

Alam has consistently denied the charges, labeling them as politically motivated. The verdict brings a significant shift in one of the most talked-about criminal cases involving a political figure in recent Nepali history.

title: MAN ACQUITTED AFTER SPENDING 5 YEARS AND 8 MONTHS IN PRISON IN FALSE RAPE CASE
content:
Biranjan Yadav, 21, lived with his sister and brother-in-law in Ghattekulo, Kathmandu. A bright student, he was studying BBA on a scholarship at Saraswati Campus. However, his life changed drastically on Bhadra 23, 2076, when he was arrested by police from the Women’s Cell, Kalimati, in a rape case.
Despite being innocent, Biranjan spent 5 years and 8 months in prison. He was finally acquitted by a joint bench of Supreme Court Justices Til Prasad Shrestha and Bal Krishna Dhakal and released from Ramechhap Prison on Jestha 2, 2082.
A teenage girl, who lived below his flat and studied in grade 9, had accused him of rape. She claimed the incident took place on Shrawan 25, 2076, in Ghattekulo after meeting him in Maitidevi. She reported it to the police about a month later.
The case went through the Kathmandu District Court, Patan High Court, and the Supreme Court. The District Court sentenced him to 12 years, which was later reduced to 7 years by the High Court.
However, key facts were ignored: the girl had lied about her name and age. The court later found she was actually over 18 at the time. Her birth certificate and educational records did not match. The defense also argued the timeline of the incident was implausible.
Dr. Gajendra Aryal and Ram Ghimire, who defended Biranjan, argued the case was based on false information and poor investigation. Dr. Aryal even represented him for free due to the family's poor financial condition.
The Supreme Court acquitted Biranjan after confirming discrepancies in the victim’s documents. He now faces another battle — to be reinstated in his hometown, Birgunj, Ward No. 18 — as he tries to rebuild his life.

title: COMPLAINT AGAINST JUDGES WHO ACQUITTED ALAM
content:
A complaint has been filed with the Judicial Council requesting an investigation and action against two High Court judges who acquitted former minister Mohammad Aftab Alam in the Rautahat bomb blast and murder case.
Yubaraj Poudel filed the complaint against Judges Dr. Khushi Prasad Tharu and Arjun Maharjan of the Birgunj bench at the Janakpur High Court. He alleges that the judges ignored the district court's verdict and the available evidence when they acquitted Alam. The complaint also calls for their immediate suspension, an investigation, and a review of their past rulings.

title: INDIA RECORDS 7 COVID DEATHS IN A DAY AND 2900+ ACTIVES CASES
content:
India's COVID-19 cases are rising again, with almost 3,000 active cases reported as of May 30. Just four days earlier, on May 26, there were only 1,010 cases. This shows a fast increase in infections.

Kerala has the highest number of cases at 1,147. After that, Maharashtra has 424 cases, Delhi has 294, and Gujarat has 223. Tamil Nadu and Karnataka both have 148 cases, while West Bengal has 116.

Other states with smaller numbers include Rajasthan (51), Uttar Pradesh (42), Puducherry (25), Haryana (20), Andhra Pradesh (16), Madhya Pradesh (10), Goa (7), and four each in Odisha, Punjab, and Jammu & Kashmir. Three cases each have been reported in Telangana, Arunachal Pradesh, and Chandigarh. Mizoram and Assam have two cases each.

No active cases have been found in Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, or the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Bihar’s data hasn’t been shared yet.

This month, at least seven people have died after testing positive for COVID-19. Two of them—one in Maharashtra and one in Delhi—had other serious health problems too. It’s still not clear if COVID-19 was the main cause of death for the others.

title: DID YOU KNOW WHO DESIGNED FLAG OF NEPAL ??
content:
The flag of Nepal is unique over the world. It is only one flag in the world which in non-quadrilateral in shape. The flag of Nepal is consisting of two triangular shapes. It has a crimson background with a dark blue border. The upper segment has a white moon emitting eight rays, with a crescent attached below. A white, stylized sun with 12 rays is in the flag's bottom section. BUT WHO DESIGNED? The flag of Nepal is designed by 89 years engineer and architect Shankar Nath Rimal. He was designed the flag on the request of King Mahendra about in 2018 BS(about 62 years ago). Rimal remembered, when king Mahendra asked him 'can you do it?, He replied 'yes, I can do it'. THIS INCIDENT CALLED HIM !! According to Rimal, after Nepal became a member of the United Nations, one flag was used when the minister went, another flag was used when the king went, and another flag was used when the secretary went. After seeing different flags, Nepal was asked, which is the official flag of Nepal? Everyone was shocked. This news reached the king. And then king Mahendra during the time of formation of New constitution in 2018, he called Rimal to design the flag.
FLAG WAS NOT ALWAYS LIKE THIS!! Before 2019, there was no standard flag in Nepal. It was customary to keep two triangles and moon and sun since tradition. Some used to put the sun above and some below to make the flag. Human faces were also placed on it. "The moon and the sun means, whatever you imagine, but the triangle, the moon and the sun, red and blue colors are what anyone would have."
HIS REMARKABLE WORKS!! He designed the attractive Shaheed Gate of the capital Kathmandu, which was inaugurated by King Mahendra on 1st Baisakh of the year 2018. Hotel Solti, Nepal Pragya-Pratishthan, Amrit Science College, Shantigriha, Sharada Sadan, Bhairahawa and Pokhara Nepal Rashtra Bank and Ramanada Chowk Janakpur Entrance gate.
HIS BACKGROUND? Rimal was Born in Tangal, Kathmandu, and he passed engineering in 1957 from Bengal Engineering College under Kolkata University. After that he was employed at Sadar Public Niksari Adda. He was also the Secretary General of Nepal Art council.

title: COLLEGE ASK STUDENTS TO TAKE OF TROUSERS BEFORE GRANTING PERIODS LEAVE
content:
A private university in Beijing has sparked outrage after a disturbing incident involving a female student. She claimed that staff at the campus clinic asked her to pull down her pants to prove she was menstruating in order to get sick leave.

The incident happened at the Gengdan Institute of Beijing University of Technology, an independent college linked to one of China’s top public universities. On May 15, the student posted a video online describing what happened. The video quickly went viral on Chinese social media.

In the video, the student is heard confronting a female staff member at the clinic, asking why such an invasive request was necessary.

“So, you're saying every woman on her period has to take off her pants and show you to get a leave note?” the student asks.

“Basically, yes. It’s not my personal rule, it’s a regulation,” the staff member replies.

When the student asks to see the regulation in writing, the staff member goes silent but continues to refuse the leave note. She tells the student to go to a hospital for proof instead.

title: PRACHANDA'S MESSAGE: RESPOND TO BRICKS WITH STONES
content:
CPN (Maoist Center) Chairman Pushpa Kamal Dahal Prachanda has said that bricks thrown by monarchists should be answered with stones.

Speaking at the Third National Conference of the Young Communist League on Sunday, Prachanda stated, “We want to live peacefully, but if we are attacked, we will respond with stones to their bricks.”

He added, “We won’t start any violence ourselves. We’ll tell the people that our movement is peaceful. But if anyone tries to attack us, we will defend ourselves. We are ready. If needed, we can even lead another rebellion.”

Prachanda explained that their ongoing campaign is a preparation for a possible future socialist revolution. “There can be no revolution without connecting with the people. What we are doing now is getting ready for that,” he said.

He also emphasized that it is the responsibility of the Maoist Center to protect the republic.

Shri Narayan Singh, the 84-year-old father of Trilok Pratap, asked, "If no one burned them in a brick kiln after putting them in sacks, then where is my son Trilok Pratap?"   [caption id="attachment_2454" align="alignnone" width="300"] Deceased Trilok Pratap's Father[/caption] He didn’t accept the High Court’s decision and demanded answers. “If the court can’t confirm my son was killed, then the government must find him,” he said. title: ROYALIST GROUP ANNOUNCED TO SHUTDOWN VALLEY
content:
A royalist group has announced a shutdown in the Kathmandu Valley on Monday, after the arrest of RPP Nepal Chairman Kamal Thapa and RPP Member of Parliament Deepak Singh.

The Joint People's Movement Committee, led by Nawaraj Subedi, released a statement on Sunday, saying that the police arrested Thapa, Singh, and others in a harsh and unfair way during a peaceful protest.

The committee has demanded that the government immediately release everyone who was arrested.

They also said the protest movement will now take a different form, and they have called for a Valley-wide shutdown on Monday (Jestha 19).

In the statement, Subedi asked supporters to actively participate in the protest by gathering in their own neighborhoods and local squares.

Leaders and activists of the RPP Nepal, including Chairman Thapa, were arrested after a royalist group protested from the Narayan Chaur area of the capital on Sunday and tried to enter Baluwatar.

title: PRACHNADA'S QUESTION TO NARAYAN KAJI: WHY DID YOU WRITE ON FACEBOOK AGAINST A JUDGE APPOINTED ON YOUR OWN RECOMMENDATION?
content: After the Birgunj bench of judges Khushi Prasad Tharu and Arjun Maharjan overturned the life sentence imposed by the Rautahat District Court, questions have been raised about the judiciary itself. The bench of Tharu and Maharjan acquitted the accused, stating that there was no solid evidence to support the claim that a bomb exploded in Alam's house on Chaitra 28, 2064, and that those injured in the explosion were loaded onto a tractor and thrown into a brick kiln to be burned. Fifteen eyewitnesses to the incident appeared before the court and testified. Following the acquittal of the culprits in such a heinous crime, the competence of the judges has been questioned. Yubaraj Poudel filed a complaint with the Judicial Council on Friday, demanding an investigation into the High Court's decision regarding Alam and action against the judges. Among the judges who made the decision, Tharu was appointed as a High Court judge from the Congress quota in 2073 BS. Tharu is also one of the 80 controversially appointed judges, known as the 'Midnight Judges.' When Sushila Karki was the chairperson of the Judicial Council, the law minister was Ajay Shankar Nayak of the Maoists. Although he was a minister, the ones who obstructed the appointment of judges were Ramesh Lekhak from the Congress and Barshaman Pun from the Maoists. Karki has publicly stated that the Ramesh Lekhak appointed other judges, including Tharu, from his party quota after a dispute with her. The same judge Tharu had acquitted Vijay Kumar Gachhadar and others in the Baluwatar case in 2080 Falgun when he was in special court. Another judge, Maharjan, who acquitted Alam, was appointed as a High Court judge from the Maoist quota on Bhadra 29, 2080. At that time, the council had recommended 27 judges for appointment to the High Court out of 56 vacancies, of which only six were from legal practitioners. Council Chairman and Chief Justice Bishwambhar Shrestha had appointed 27 people as judges of the High Court amid controversy after a prolonged vacancy. Maharjan, who worked in the firm of former Nepal Bar President Chandeshwor Shrestha, became a judge from the quota of the Maoists, led by the then-government. According to sources, the then-Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister Narayan Kaji Shrestha played a decisive role in his appointment as a judge. At that time, Prachanda was the Prime Minister under the Congress-Maoist alliance, and Dhanraj Gurung was the Law Minister.

title: MAN CHOPPED SISTER IN LAW HEAD OVER FAMILY DISPUTE
content:
May 31, 2025, in West Bengal's South 24 Parganas district, specifically in the Bharatgarh area of Basanti. The man, identified as Bimal Mondal, was arrested after he was seen walking through the streets carrying the severed head of his sister-in-law, named Sati Mondal or Pratima Mondal in different reports, along with a chopper or sickle-like weapon used in the crime.

The murder stemmed from a family dispute, possibly related to property issues or longstanding tensions, which escalated into a violent altercation. Locals alerted the police after witnessing the gruesome scene, and some recorded videos of Bimal walking with the severed head. He reportedly walked nearly three miles toward the Basanti police station, where he surrendered, still carrying the head and the weapon.

The victim's body was found in a field, and the police have sent it for post-mortem examination while seizing the murder weapon. Initial investigations suggest the crime occurred late Friday night or early Saturday morning, with a forensic team now examining the scene.

Eyewitnesses noted Bimal's intense rage, as he was heard cursing the victim and her husband, claiming he was avenging years of perceived injustice. The local community is in shock, as frequent quarrels between Bimal and the victim had been reported, but no one anticipated such a horrific act.

title: WRIT IN SUPREME COURT AGAINST PUBLIC TRANSPORT STRIKE
content:
A writ petition has been filed in the Supreme Court against the public transport strike called by the National Federation of Nepal Transport Entrepreneurs. On Tuesday, advocate Bivek Pokharel filed the petition, naming the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport, and the Federation as defendants.

The petition is scheduled for hearing on Wednesday. It seeks an interim order to immediately resume public transport services, arguing that the strike violates the Constitution. Public transport is classified as an essential service, and strikes in such sectors are prohibited by law.

The petition claims that the strike has violated the fundamental rights of citizens by restricting their freedom of movement, profession, and employment rights that are guaranteed under Article 17, Sub article 2 of the Constitution.

title: EMERGENCY MEETING CALLED TO INITIATE INVESTIGATION
content:
An emergency meeting of the Judicial Council is scheduled to be held to initiate the investigation process against the judges who acquitted Nepali Congress MP Mohammad Aftab Alam in a murder case.

Judicial Council Chairman and Chief Justice Prakash Man Singh Raut has directed that an emergency meeting be convened at 9 AM on Wednesday. "The agenda of the meeting will include the appointment of judges and other matters, but the primary focus will be the decision to acquit Alam," a Judicial Council source said. "Today's meeting is likely to concentrate on this issue."

A few days ago, during an informal "zero hour" meeting of the Supreme Court judges, this issue was raised loudly and seriously. After questions began to arise from all sides, the Chief Justice, in consultation with the council members, fixed the date for the meeting.

The Judicial Council, led by Chief Justice Prakash Man Singh Raut, includes the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court, Sapana Pradhan Malla; members Ram Prasad Bhandari and Damodar Khadka; and Law Minister Ajay Kumar Chaurasia.

title: MURDER CASE AGAINST EX SPEAKER REVIVED
content:
The Constitutional Bench of the Supreme Court has issued a mandamus order against former Speaker Agni Sapkota in connection with a murder case.

With this order, the path has now opened for investigation and prosecution of Sapkota in the case of the abduction and subsequent murder of Arjun Lama from Kavre.

According to the Supreme Court's website, the order was issued on Wednesday by a Constitutional Bench comprising Chief Justice Prakashman Singh Raut, along with Justices Sapana Pradhan Malla, Kumar Regmi, Manoj Kumar Sharma, and Kumar Chudal.

A writ petition had been filed by journalist Kanak Mani Dixit, Arjun Lama’s wife Purnimaya Lama, and human rights activist Sushil Pyakurel, demanding justice and punishment for Sapkota, accusing him of involvement in Lama’s abduction and murder in Kavre.

Purnimaya Lama had initially filed the case against Sapkota in 2069 BS (2012 AD), alleging his involvement in the murder of her husband. At the time the case was filed, Sapkota had been appointed Minister of Information and Communications.

Arjun Lama had been abducted and killed in Kavre in 2062 BS (2005 AD). Sapkota has consistently denied the allegations, arguing that the case should be treated as a conflict-era incident and therefore not subject to regular criminal prosecution.

title: Four Nepali Family Members Found Dead in Virginia, USA
content: Four members of a Nepali family were found dead inside their apartment in Manassas Park, Virginia, on Thursday night. The victims include a 38-year-old man, a 36-year-old woman, their 8-year-old daughter, and 2-year-old son. Police said all four died from gunshot wounds. A gun was found at the scene. The family members have been identified as Santosh Pariyar, Anju Shrestha, and their two children. The police were called to the apartment around 10:40 PM after the landlord became worried. The landlord said he had not heard from the family for several days. When police entered the home, they found all four people dead. Officers say the case may be a murder-suicide, but they have not confirmed who fired the gun. The bodies have been sent for post-mortem examination, and the investigation is still ongoing. Neighbors told police that the family had moved to the U.S. from Nepal about six months ago. The Nepali community in the area is deeply saddened by the incident.

title: Pakistan Begs to India for water
content:
Pakistan has asked India for the fourth time to rethink its decision to stop the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT). India suspended the treaty after a terrorist attack in Pahalgam on April 22, which killed 26 people.

Pakistan is facing a serious water shortage and is urgently trying to restart the treat. Even after India carried out Operation Sindoor, Pakistan continued to send requests about the treaty.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has made it clear that India will not hold talks while terrorism continues. He said, "Water and blood cannot flow together" and "talks and terror cannot go on at the same time."

title: Show Cause order in the name of Nepal Electricity Authority
content: The bench of Honorable Judge Shree Durga Prasad Dhungel has issued a show cause order in the name of Nepal Electricity Authority, Central Office. On Sunday, a law student, Bivek Chaudhary, filed a writ petition in the Patan High Court demanding to give prior notice to the consumers before cutting the electricity. Petitioner has mentioned that Article 27 of our constitution has provisioned for the right to information, and it is the right of the consumers to get prior notice before a power cut.  The petitioner argues that such prior notice would not only uphold consumers' rights but also promote transparency and accountability in the operations of the Nepal Electricity Authority. The hearing of the writ was scheduled on Monday, where Patan High Court issued a show cause order in the name of the defendant. The court has directed the defendant to explain why such notices have not been issued to consumers, emphasizing the importance of transparency and communication in public services. This case could set a significant precedent for consumer rights and accountability in utility management.

title: 3 out of 4 people who give money to friends Never get it back
content:
A survey conducted by LendingTree has revealed a troubling trend that those who have loaned money to friends or family, about 73% have yet to be repaid in full.

That means nearly three in four people who extended loans in good faith are still waiting for their money back. Beyond financial loss, this repayment gap is taking a toll on relationships, 25% of respondents reported that the unpaid debt damaged their relationship, while 43% expressed regret for having borrowed in the first place.

Most of these loans were made informally, often with no written contracts, repayment schedule, or interest terms. This casual approach may ease lending in the moment but frequently leads to tension later. In LendingTree’s findings, the lack of clarity and structure has resulted in not only financial shortfalls but also emotional strain among loved ones.

Financial advisors emphasize that loans between friends or family should be approached as seriously as any business agreement. They recommend setting clear terms, such as repayment timelines, amounts, and consequences for default—and documenting them in writing. This transparency helps align expectations and reduce potential friction.

A recent MarketWatch story illustrates how even generous lending can have unintended fallout. One individual recounted lending $120,000 across relationships, tenants, friends, and family only to suffer emotional exhaustion and financial loss. Experts in the story urged setting firm boundaries and only lending money you’re prepared to lose.

title: Judicial Council recommended for the removal of Two Judges
content:
Judicial Council has recommended the Supreme Court (SC) to recall two judges from the temporary bench of Janakpur High Court in Birgunj, who had acquitted Nepali Congress leader and former minister Mohammad Aftab Alam and three others.

Judges Dr Khusi Prasad Tharu and Arjun Maharjan had delivered the controversial verdict, clearing Alam of charges in the infamous Rautahat bomb blast case. Following the verdict, complaints were filed against both judges by the victims' father Srinarayan Singh Rajput and legal activists Yubaraj Safal , demanding an investigation.

The recommendation for their removal was made during Wednesday’s meeting of the Judicial Council. However, Registrar of the Birgunj bench, Dipak Bhandari, said they have yet to receive an official letter confirming the decision.

title: Supreme Court ruled to remove tax on Sanitary Pad
content:
Supreme Court of Nepal on Wednesday, comprising the justices Manoj Kumar Sharma and Mahesh Sharma Poudel issued the decision in response to a writ petition filed by two law students, Shreena Nepal and Abhyuday Bherwal from Kathmandu School of Law, claiming to remove tax from Sanitary pad.

The writ was filed on 2078, Shrawan 26 and after four year of legal hearing court issued the decision to remove the tax on sanitary pad.

The students were demanded to remove tax from menstrual products, arguing that they are essential goods rather than luxury items.

According to the department of customs, imported sanitary pads currently carry a total 18% of tax- 5% customs duty and 13% value added tax (VAT).

“The full text of the verdict has yet to be released, but once the decision is enforced, it will help promote domestic production, lower prices of sanitary pads, and potentially increase exports,” said Dol Raj Adhikari, president of the Nepal Sanitary and Diaper Association.

“With this ruling, sanitary pads will become 18 percent cheaper. For example, a packet priced at Rs.60 will now cost approximately Rs.50 after tax removal,”.

He added that it remains unclear whether both VAT and customs duties have been removed for imported products as well.

title: Senior Advocate Meera Dhungana Stresses Law Alone Isn’t Enough Without Implementation and Awareness
content: Kathmandu, June 22 – “Laws alone are not enough; without effective implementation and social awareness, change is impossible,” said senior advocate Meera Dhungana at a special event organized by NaLC Feminist Spark titled ‘Feminist Voice in Law: A Conversation with Meera Dhungana’. She emphasized that modern forms of violence against women—mental, economic, cyber, and social exclusion—often go unaddressed by current legal frameworks. Dhungana highlighted the gap between society and the justice system, calling for collective and individual efforts to bridge it. The event saw active participation from female legal professionals, students, and activists, with an interactive session moderated by Prashna Mahat. Participants expressed hope that such discussions would strengthen perspectives on women's rights and access to justice. NALC Feminist Spark is a student-led club at National Law College dedicated to advocating for women's rights, gender justice, equality, and the empowerment of women. Founded and run by passionate students, the club serves as a platform to raise awareness, challenge stereotypes, and promote inclusive dialogue on campus. Through workshops, discussions, campaigns, and outreach programs, Feminist Spark encourages students—especially young women—to lead with confidence and drive meaningful change in society. Guided by its powerful slogan, “Women can lead and can bring change,” the club stands as a beacon of progressive thought, aiming to build a more just, equal, and empowered future for all.

title: Cyber case against journalist Dilbhusan Pathak
content: A case has been filed in the name of Journalist Dilbhusan Pathak for Cyber Crime. The District Government Attorney's Office, Kathmandu, has filed a case against Pathak, seeking punishment under Section 47 (1) of the Electronic Transactions Act 2063 BS. The case has been filed at Kathmandu District Court seeking fine of one lakh rupees or five years imprisonment, or both for publishing illegal materials in electronic means. Earlier on Jestha 28, arrest warrant issued againt Pathak, for publishing video showing Jaybir, son of Nepali Congress President Sher Bahadur Deuba, about to purchase Hilton Hotel. The Cyber ​​Bureau had obtained the arrest warrant from the court after Jaybir filed a complaint claiming that the video posted on YouTube was baseless. However, Patan high court on Asar 5 give an interim order not arrest Pathak.

title: Supreme Court- Open University students should participate in the advocate's license exam
content:
Supreme Court says, Open University students should participate in the advocate's license exam. The Supreme Court has issued an interim order to allow students who have passed LLB from the Open University to participate in the advocate's license examination on Thursday. The Bar Council had issued a notice prohibiting Open University students from filling out the licensing exam form.
The deadline to fill out the form for the advocate license exam is Asar 21. The students had gone to the Supreme Court after they were unable to fill out the form. A bench of Justices Kumar Regmi and Til Prasad Shrestha ordered not to deprive them from filling out the form and participating in the examination.

title: Same sex marriage in Nepal Arghakhachi
content: Two young women studying at the graduation level in Arghakhachi have married to each other. After the wedding, the couple also got their same-sex marriage registered at the ward office. Anita from Bhumikasthan Municipality in Arghakhanchi and Binita (name changed) from Kapilvastu Municipality in Kapilvastu got married on 18 Jestha 2082 after falling in love while studying in college. Jyoti Panthi, ward secretary of Bhumikasthan Municipality-9, said that 23-year-old Anita from Arghakhanchi became the groom and 20-year-old Binita the bride and registered a 'same-sex marriage' in handwritten form. After their marriage, they have been living in Kapilvastu. 'Initially, there was some confusion, but later, after understanding from the municipality, we gave them a handwritten marriage registration certificate,' she said. 'We have not made it public as both of them asked to keep their names confidential.'

title: All about Nepal Bar Association- History, Functions, Structures
content:
Nepal Bar Association is the Guardian of Legal Profession and Judicial Independence because it plays a WATCHDOG Role in upholding the RULE OF LAW, Professional Integrity, and Judicial Accountability. The NBA exists not just to organize lawyers, but to the safeguard the judicial system itself – making it a keystone institution in a constitutional democracy. The main Reason behind the Establishment of the Nepal Bar Association (NBA) in 1956 (2013 BS) was to create a unified, professional body to regulate and uplift the legal profession in Nepal at a time when legal education was still in its infancy. Back then most lawyers were licensed based on Practical experience, not formal legal education. The NBA was formed to:
  1. Promote legal education and training,
  2. Enforce Ethical Standards among lawyers,
  3. Advocate for the rule of law and judicial independence, and Represent the collective voice of legal professionals.
In essence, the NBA emerged as a guardian of legal professionalism and justice, laying the foundation for a modern, accountable legal system in Nepal. Hence, The Nepal Bar Association is the Federal Organization of Practicing lawyers in Nepal. It serves as the Umbrella body for all bar units across the country and is governed by a Central Executive Committee elected through direct voting by its members. The First President of the Nepal Bar Association was Devnath Prasad Verma, Nepal's first licensed senior advocate. He was Pioneer in private legal practice and laid the foundation for organized legal advocacy in the country.  As of April 2025, the current president is Senior Advocate Prof. Dr. Bijaya Prasad Mishara, elected with a strong mandate from legal professional across Nepal.  The Nepal Bar Association (NBA), established in 1956, currently has around 12,000 members, including senior advocates, advocates, and pleaders. Structure of NBA: Membership in the NBA is typically composed of licensed legal practitioners, and the association is structured with a Central working Committee through direct voting by its members. The NBA is led by 25 elected members, and any qualified lawyer in Nepal can voluntarily become a member. The Nepal Bar Association (NBA) has a Central Executive Committee composed of over 25 members, representing various provinces, legal communities, and interest groups.  Key members executive lineup:
  1. President
  2. General Secretary
  3. Treasurer
  4. Vice Presidents (One from each province & female):
  5. 14 other executive members
The Central Executive Committee of the Nepal Bar Association (NBA), which includes 25 members, is elected for a term of 2 years. This 2-year term ensures regular leadership renewal and representation across Nepal’s diverse legal landscape. The President of the Nepal Bar Association is a senior elected advocate who leads the national body of legal professionals.  This person automatically becomes the Vice-Chairperson of the Nepal Bar Council. All registered members of the NBA vote directly to elect the executive committee. The committee includes a President, multiple Vice-Presidents (representing provinces and specific groups), a Secretary General, Treasurer, and 14 other members representing various legal communities and regions. Every court in Nepal (District court, High court, Supreme Court) has its own local bar unit. Functions of NBA: The Nepal Bar Association (NBA) plays a vital role in the legal landscape of Nepal. Its functions includes:
  1. Promotes the interest of lawyers
  2. Provides legal aid services
  3. Advocates for law reform
  4. Represents lawyers in dealings with the government
  5. Trains legal Practitioners.
NBR has no statutory powers, influences legislation and policy through advocacy it means that Nepal bar association doesn't have legal authority granted by law to make or enforce rules like a government body does. It can't pass laws or force anyone to follow its decisions. But through advocacy – which includes speaking out, giving expert opinions, organizing events, and influencing public opinion – it can shape laws and policies. It acts like a powerful voice in the room, not the rule – maker, but the one who helps guide those who make the rules. i.e. Think of it as a Respected coach in a game : it can't change the rules, but it's advice and reputation influence how the game is played . Example of NBA Work: Cholendra Shumsher JB Rana One of the most high – profile and controversial case involving the Nepal bar association (NBA) submitted a 35 – point letter to  the impeachment Recommendation Committee, detailing alleged misconduct by CJ Rana . The NBA accused him for manipulating judicial appointments and seeking bribes for judge transfers and promotion. Nepal Bar Association operates under several key legal frameworks: Nepal Bar Council Act, 2050 (1993): Establishes the Nepal Bar Council and outlines its structure, powers, and duties. Legal Aid Act, 2054 (1997): Recognizes NBA’s role in providing legal aid; NBA’s President and Secretary are ex-officio members of the Central Legal Aid Committee. Professional Conduct Rules (2079): Sets ethical standards for legal practitioners. Current Executive Committee of NBA: As of April 2025, the Nepal Bar Association (NBA) is led by senior Advocate Dr. Bijaya Prasad Mishara, who was elected president after securing votes. President Mishara has pledged to clean up the judiciary and promote transparency, signaling a stronger stance on accountability and reform. President: Senior Advocate Prof. Dr. Bijay Prasad Mishra General Secretary: Senior Advocate Kedar Prasad Koirala Treasurer: Senior Advocate Jagat Bahadur Karki Vice Presidents (by region and representation): Koshi province: Advocate Padam Prasad Limbu Madhesh Province: Advocate Ajay Shankar Jha Bagmati Province: Advocate Tej Bahadur Rawal Gandaki Province: Advocate Bhupendra Khanal Lumbini Province: Advocate Krishna Prasad Pokharel Karnali Province: Advocate Bibash Kumar Basnet Sudurpaschim Province: Advocate Siddharaj Ojha Female Category: Advocate Saraswati Shrestha Other Executive Committee Members Senior Advocate Rajkumar Shrestha Advocate Mangal Sundar Shilpakar Advocate Kiran Neupane Advocate Sharada Gurung Advocate Daman Bahadur Chand Advocate Baburam Aryal Advocate Suryakumar Yadav Advocate Dr. Mukunda Adhikari Advocate Ranjita Karki Advocate Madhav Mainali Advocate Rinku Kumari Yadav Advocate Kiran Poudel Advocate Indira Acharya Advocate Chiranjivi Tilkyani

title: If a man feels that he cannot maintain his wife and family, he should not marry...
content: Case: Tej Bahadur Maurya vs. Smt. Nisha Maurya Date: 7 April 2026 Background of the Case: Dispute arose from an order passed by Family Court, Prayagraj, under Section 24 of Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Family Court had directed husband to pay ₹4,000 per month to his wife as interim maintenance (maintenance pendente lite) during pendency of matrimonial proceedings. Aggrieved by this order, husband approached Allahabad High Court by filing an appeal. Appeal filed by husband was delayed by 72 days. High Court, after considering the reasons mentioned in application, condoned delay and allowed matter to be heard on merits. Accordingly, delay condonation application was allowed. Arguments by the Husband (Appellant): Husband argued that he is merely a labourer with very limited income and is not in a position to pay ₹4,000 per month as maintenance. He contended that trial court failed to properly consider his financial condition and liabilities. He further submitted that he had already placed details regarding his income, expenditure, and other responsibilities before the trial court. Additionally, he alleged that his wife is living with another man and that there was a mutual separation between them, supported by an affidavit, which according to him was ignored by the trial court. Stand of the Wife (Respondent): Wife opposed the submissions made by husband and stated that allegations levelled against her were false, fabricated, and intended to defame her. She submitted that affidavit referred by husband had been obtained through deceit, particularly as she is not well educated. She also emphasized that she has no independent source of income and is dependent on maintenance for her survival and to support her responsibilities. Observations of the High Court: Upon examining the record, High Court observed that trial court had duly considered submissions made by both parties before passing impugned order. Court held that the allegations raised by husband involve disputed questions of fact, which can only be properly adjudicated during course of trial and not at the stage of interim maintenance. It reiterated that under Section 24 of Hindu Marriage Act, either spouse who lacks sufficient independent income is entitled to maintenance during pendency of proceedings. Court further observed that mere assertion of financial hardship is not sufficient, and such claims must be substantiated with credible evidence. Key Remark by the Court: In a significant observation, Court remarked that if a man feels that he is not in a position to maintain his wife and family, he should not enter into marriage. This observation underscores the legal and moral responsibility that accompanies the institution of marriage. Final Decision: After considering the entire matter, High Court concluded that there was no material infirmity in order passed by Family Court. Court held that amount of ₹4,000 per month awarded as maintenance is reasonable, especially in view of the prevailing cost of living, and cannot be said to be excessive or unaffordable. Consequently, appeal filed by husband was dismissed, and order directing payment of maintenance, along with arrears as previously determined, was upheld. Legal Significance: This judgment reaffirms settled legal position that maintenance is a binding obligation arising out of marriage. It highlights that unsubstantiated allegations cannot be used as a ground to deny interim maintenance and that financial incapacity must be proved with cogent evidence. The ruling also reinforces the principle that courts will ensure financial support to a dependent spouse during litigation, in order to maintain fairness and dignity in matrimonial proceedings

title: Contract law case: Bijaya Kumar Shah v. Excise Department, Kathmandu & Others, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Contract law case: Bijaya Kumar Shah v. Excise Department, Kathmandu & Others, NKP 2049, Issue 5, D. No.: 4531.   Case: Injunction relating to enforcement of contractual obligations Plaintiff: Bijaya Kumar Shah Defendant: Excise Department (Kathmandu), Excise Office (Chitwan), Ministry of Finance. Decision No: 4531  

This case is related to Injunction relating to enforcement of contractual obligations and recovery of excise-related dues, performance of contract.

  Facts of the Case: The Excise Department invited applications to establish and operate a distillery. Bijaya Kumar Shah agreed to establish the distillery by depositing Rs. 5,56,750/- as security and accepting the condition that he would pay a minimum annual excise duty of Rs. 2,227,000/-. According to the agreement, he had to complete the distillery and begin production within the prescribed time. If he failed to do so, the security deposit would be forfeited. He was also allowed to operate temporarily while paying excise duty in installments. While constructing the distillery, heavy rainfall caused the reservoir to be washed away and the land to collapse. Before the original deadline expired he requested an extension. The Excise Department granted only a two-month extension, but he still could not complete the project. The government later cancelled his license, forfeited his security deposit, and demanded payment of the remaining excise amount. Fearing that his property would be seized to recover the amount, Bijaya Kumar Shah filed a petition seeking an injunction to stop the government from recovering the money. Plaintiff's Claim: He could not complete the distillery because of natural disasters, which made performance impossible. Since no liquor was produced, excise duty should not be charged. The contract had become impossible to perform, so forfeiting his security deposit and recovering additional excise duty was unlawful. The government's recovery process threatened his property rights protected under the Civil Rights Act, 2012 B.S. Therefore, court should issue an injunction preventing the government from recovering the claimed amount. Defendant's Arguments: Plaintiff voluntarily entered into the contract and accepted all its terms. He failed to establish the distillery within the agreed time. Under the agreement, failure to complete the project resulted in automatic forfeiture of the security deposit. The government lawfully cancelled license and initiated recovery of the remaining excise amount according to contract and applicable laws. Since the authorities were only enforcing the contractual terms, there was no violation of any fundamental or civil right, and therefore an injunction could not be granted.   Legal Issues:
  1. Can a person avoid contractual obligations because the agreed project could not be completed?
  1. Can an injunction be issued to stop the government from recovering money that is due under a voluntarily signed contract?
  2. Does enforcement of contractual liabilities amount to a violation of rights protected under the Civil Rights Act, 2012?
  Decisions of Courts: Bagmati Zonal Court: Zonal Court held that Excise Department had not properly followed the contractual provision regarding further extension of time and allowed petition and ordered the issuance of an injunction. Madhyamanchal Regional Court: Regional Court reversed Bagmati Zonal Court's decision and held that the government was merely enforcing the contract voluntarily signed by petitioner. Since no protected civil right was threatened, the injunction was refused and the petition was dismissed. Supreme Court: Supreme Court dismissed appeal also held that Bijaya Kumar Shah voluntarily entered into the agreement and remained bound by its terms so, the forfeiture of security deposit and recovery of the remaining amount were actions taken under the contract. Such recovery did not violate any right protected by the Civil Rights Act. Therefore, no injunction could be granted and the decision of Madhyamanchal Regional Court was affirmed.   Established Principles:
  1. A person who voluntarily enters into a contract must perform the contractual obligations within the agreed time.
  2. A contracting party cannot escape liabilities arising from the agreement simply because performance was not completed.
  3. Recovery of money due under a valid contract does not violate civil rights protected under the Civil Rights Act.
  4. An injunction cannot be granted merely to prevent lawful enforcement of contractual obligations.
  5. Where there is no actual or threatened violation of a protected legal right, the remedy of injunction is not available.

title: Contract Law Case: Pradeep Kumar Kedia v. Ministry of Forests & Others NKP 2046 (5th Semester)
content:
Contract Law Case: Pradeep Kumar Kedia v. Ministry of Forests & Others NKP 2046, No. 11, P. 1183, D.No: 4009   Case: Compensation for Damages, Partial performance of a contract. Plaintiff: Pradeep Kumar Kedia Defendants: Ministry of Forests, Kathmandu and Others. Decision Number: 4009  

This Case is related to claim for Compensation, Partial performance of a contract.

  Facts of the Case: Plaintiff entered into a contract with govt of Nepal on 18 Chaitra 2034 to purchase and remove marked trees from four forest plots in the Rapti Forest Division. He deposited Rs. 80,000/- as security and began cutting, transporting, and stacking the timber. During the work, heavy rainfall started earlier than expected, making roads and rivers impassable because of these natural conditions, plaintiff could not complete the work within the contractual time. He requested an extension until Jestha 2036 according to the contract. Before deciding on his request, the government cancelled the contract, confiscated all timber remaining in the forest and stacked timber, and also forfeited his Rs. 80,000/- security deposit. Plaintiff then claimed that this caused him a loss of Rs. 5,80,000/- and filed a suit seeking compensation and return of the security deposit.   Plaintiff's Claim: Plaintiff argued that, Heavy rainfall prevented timely completion of the work and he had already applied for an extension as allowed by the contract. The government cancelled the contract before deciding on his extension request and argued that the cancellation, confiscation of timber, and forfeiture of the security deposit were illegal. Therefore, he should receive Rs. 5,00,000/- as compensation for losses and Rs. 80,000/- as refund of the security deposit.   Defendants' Arguments: Defendants argued that, plaintiff failed to complete even 60% of the required work within the agreed period and violated the contractual conditions. According to the contract, the government had the authority to cancel the contract and confiscate the security deposit. Therefore, plaintiff had no legal right to claim compensation or refund of the deposit.   Legal Issues:
  1. Whether the Government could legally cancel the contract and confiscate the security deposit even though the contractor had partially completed the work and still had contractual time remaining to remove the timber stacked at the depot?
  Decisions of Courts: Narayani Zonal Court: Zonal Court dismissed plaintiff's claim and held that the government had acted according to the contract and plaintiff was not entitled to compensation or refund of the security deposit. Madhyamanchal Regional Court: Regional Court upheld the decision of Narayani Zonal Court also held that plaintiff had failed to perform the contract within the stipulated time and therefore could not claim damages. Supreme Court: Supreme Court Partly allowed the appeal also held that although plaintiff had not fully completed the contract, ordered the government to refund the security deposit of Rs. 80,000/- and rejected plaintiff's claim for the remaining compensation of Rs. 5,00,000/-.   Established Principles:
  1. Partial performance of a contract must be given legal effect where the contract itself recognizes separate stages of performance.
  2. If timber has already been transported to the depot, and the contract allows a separate period for its removal after payment, the contractor retains the right to remove that timber during the remaining contractual period.
  3. The Government cannot prematurely terminate the contract and forfeit the security deposit before the expiry of the contractual period for removing depot-stacked timber.
  4. Although the contractor may not be entitled to full compensation for all claimed losses, the security deposit cannot be forfeited when contractual rights still remain.

title: Contract Law Case: Swamilal Shrestha vs. Nepal oil corporation NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Contract Law Case: Swamilal Shrestha vs. Nepal oil corporation NKP 2055, No.6, P.340   Case: Loan Transaction, obligation and liability of guarantors/sureties. Plaintiff: Nepal oil Corporation Defendants: Swamilal Shrestha and Mohan Lal Shrestha Decision No: 6559  

The case is related with enforcement of a contractual obligation and liability of guarantors/sureties.

  Facts of the case: On 2026/09/28 B.S., NOC entered into a written agreement with contractors Swamilal Shrestha and Mohan Lal Shrestha. Under the agreement, the contractors were required to supply 600,000 man (मन) of firewood at the rate of Rs. 4.15 per man. NOC provided them with 12 diesel trucks belonging to the Corporation and also gave them Rs. 200,000/- as an advance. It was agreed that after the contractors completed the required work and supplied the agreed quantity of firewood, the 12 trucks would be transferred into their names. However, if they failed to complete the work, the Corporation had the right to confiscate the trucks. The contractors were also responsible for any damage or loss to the trucks. On 2026/11/09 B.S., several persons stood as property guarantors for the obligations of the contractors, while Mahanta Lal stood as a money guarantor. The guarantee covered the value of the trucks and the money involved in the transaction. Despite repeated demands from the Corporation, the contractors failed to complete the contractual work. Additional amounts were also received on behalf of the contractors, and further guarantee documents were executed in connection with those amounts. Ultimately, the Corporation determined that the contractors had failed to perform their contractual obligations. Its Board decided that the Corporation should recover Rs. 246,012/-, representing the value of the 12 trucks, and Rs. 182,336/-, representing the amount remaining payable according to the Corporation's accounts. On this basis, the Corporation filed a suit seeking recovery of a total amount of Rs. 428,348/- from the contractors and the guarantors.   Plaintiff's Claim: NOC claimed that the contractors had received the 12 trucks and Rs. 200,000/- advance under the written contract but failed to complete the agreed firewood-supply work and failed to properly return the trucks. They also failed to pay the outstanding amount shown in the Corporation's accounts, despite defendants having executed guarantee documents for the contractors' obligations. Therefore, the Corporation sought to recover Rs. 246,012/- for the 12 trucks and Rs. 182,336/- as the outstanding amount, totaling Rs. 428,348/-, from the contractors and guarantors.   Defendants' Arguments: Defendants argued that the guarantors could not be directly sued before the principal contractors, because their liability was secondary. The Corporation should first proceed against Swamilal Shrestha and Mohan Lal Shrestha and their property, and only if the amount could not be recovered should it proceed against the guarantors. They also argued that the claim was barred by limitation and that the case had been filed in the wrong court, as it should have been filed before Zonal Court rather than District Court. The contractors further claimed that the failure to complete the contract was not their fault because the Corporation had failed to provide the required forest plots. They also maintained that the accounts relating to the trucks had already been settled.   Legal Issues:
  1. Can a creditor directly sue both the principal debtor and the guarantor in the same action without first proceeding against the principal debtor?
  2. What is the extent of a guarantor's liability under the law relating to surety?
  3. What amount was actually recoverable by the plaintiff after accounting for the trucks and amounts payable to the contractors?
  Decision of Courts: Kathmandu District Court: Kathmandu District Court dismissed plaintiff's suit because it was filed in the wrong court. Court held that, under Section 15(2) of the Corporation Act, 2021, a case involving the NOC should be heard by the competent Zonal Court, not by District Court. Therefore, District Court held that it lacked jurisdiction to hear the case. Reconsideration: Plaintiff sought reconsideration of the dismissal because the case had been rejected due to a jurisdictional error. A Hukum Pramangi was issued directing that the case be examined by the competent court. The basic reasoning was that a party should not lose its substantive legal right merely because of a procedural or jurisdictional mistake by the court.   Bagmati Zonal Court: Bagmati Zonal Court held that plaintiff was entitled to recover Rs. 428,348/- from the contractors and guarantors. Court also found that the contract existed, the contractors had received the 12 trucks and money, the guarantee documents had been executed, and the contractors had failed to complete their contractual obligations. Therefore, court ordered recovery of the claimed amount of Rs. 428,348/- from defendants.   Patan Appellate Court: Defendants appealed against the decision of the Bagmati Zonal Court. Patan Appellate Court partly reversed the earlier decision and determined that the amount actually recoverable was Rs. 151,054/-, instead of the full amount claimed. The court applied the legal rule concerning the liability of guarantors and held that the principal contractors must first be proceeded against, and only if the amount could not be recovered from them could the guarantors be proceeded against. Therefore, plaintiff could not directly recover the amount from guarantors in the same manner as from the principal debtors, and the earlier judgment was modified accordingly.   Supreme Court Decision: Supreme Court upheld the decision of Patan Appellate Court and dismissed defendants’ appeal. It confirmed that plaintiff was entitled to recover Rs. 151,054/-, but the recovery had to be made according to Section 6 of the Jamani Garneko Mahal, which requires the principal debtors to be proceeded against first and the guarantors only according to the prescribed legal procedure.   Established Principles:
  1. Principal debtor must be proceeded against first: Under Section 6 of the Jamani Garneko Mahal, when a debt is guaranteed, the creditor must first proceed against the principal debtor and his property.
  2. Guarantor's liability is secondary: The guarantor becomes liable only after the legal procedure for recovery from the principal debtor has been followed and the amount remains unrecovered.
  3. No double recovery for the same property: Since the 12 trucks had already been taken back by the Fuel Corporation, their value could not again be recovered from the defendants. The Corporation could not both retain the trucks and claim their full value as an outstanding amount.

title: Contract Law Case: Madan Bahadur Thapa vs. Khindra Bahadur Thapa, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Contract Law Case: Madan Bahadur Thapa vs. Khindra Bahadur Thapa, NKP, 2060, No. 3/4, P. 178, D.No. 7187   Case: Loan Transaction, Debt Recovery Plaintiff: Madan Bahadur Thapa Defendant: Khindra Bahadur Thapa Decision No: 7187  

This case is related to execution of loan deed, Loan Transaction.

  Facts of the Case: On 2050/11/24 B.S. defendant borrowed Rs. 43,875/- from plaintiff and executed a loan deed. Plaintiff claimed that defendant failed to repay both principal and interest within the agreed period. Defendant admitted signing the loan deed but stated that the loan originally began in 2049/02/05 B.S. and the deed dated 2050/11/24 B.S was only a renewed document extending the repayment period. He claimed that he had already repaid Rs. 15,000/- and for the remaining Rs. 29,000/- both parties executed a contract on 2051/05/01 B.S. under which he agreed to transfer his land to plaintiff. Plaintiff later obtained a court judgment recognizing his ownership over that land. Therefore, according to defendant, no loan amount remained payable. The dispute arose because plaintiff still sought recovery of the entire loan based on the loan deed, while defendant argued that the later land contract had already settled the remaining debt.   Plaintiff's Claim: Defendant borrowed Rs. 43,875/- under a loan deed dated 2050/11/24 B.S. and failed to repay the loan within the agreed time. Therefore, plaintiff demanded principal amount together with accrued interest and continuing legal interest until payment.   Defendant's Arguments: The loan deed of 2050/11/24 B.S. was only a renewal of an earlier loan and he had already repaid Rs. 15,000/- The remaining Rs. 29,000/- was settled through the contract dated 2051/05/01 B.S. under which he agreed to transfer his land to plaintiff and he had already obtained a court judgment recognizing ownership over that land Therefore, the earlier loan obligation had already been settled and no further payment was due.   Legal Issues:
  1. Does a later contract for transfer of land between the same parties settle and replace an earlier loan agreement?
  Decisions of the Courts: Makwanpur District Court: District court held that defendant failed to prove repayment of the loan and ordered defendant to pay the principal and interest according to the loan deed. Hetauda Appellate Court: Held that the later contract regarding the land settled the earlier loan transaction and reversed District Court's judgment. Supreme Court (Joint Bench): Justice Harish Chandra Prasad Upadhyaya: Restored District Court's decision. Justice Kedar Nath Acharya: Uphold Appellate Court's decision. Supreme Court (Full Bench): It held that although the loan deed and the later contract were different legal documents, they involved the same parties and formed part of the same financial arrangement. Since the later contract was intended to settle the outstanding debt by transferring land, Plaintiff could not claim the loan amount again under the earlier loan deed and upheld Appellate Court's judgment and dismissed plaintiff’s claim.   Established Principles: A loan deed and a contract are different legal documents, but when they are executed between the same parties as part of the same financial transaction, they must be read together. If the later agreement was intended to settle the earlier debt, the creditor cannot recover the same debt again under the earlier loan deed.

title: Contract Law Case: Education and Sports Ministry v. S.P. Nepal Enterprises and Others, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Contract Law Case: Education and Sports Ministry v. S.P. Nepal Enterprises and Others, NKP, 2069, No. 12, P. 1854, D.No. 8935   Case: Guarantee of contract. Plaintiff: S.P. Nepal Enterprises, Gongabu, Kathmandu Defendant: Government of Nepal, Ministry of Education and Sports, National Sports Council (Rastriya Khelkud Parishad) Decision Number: 8935  

This case is related to guarantor of loan.

  Facts of the Case: The Government invited tenders to sell tickets for the 8th South Asian Games. S.P. Nepal Enterprises submitted the successful bid and deposited a bank guarantee. Later, the Government informed the company that it could not provide all the tickets and seats originally promised. Therefore, both parties signed a revised contract reducing the number of tickets to be supplied. plaintiff sold the tickets received and argued that after deducting the value of the tickets that were never supplied and the tickets taken by the Police and the All Nepal Football Association, it had already paid all the money required under the contract and plaintiff further claimed that it had even overpaid a small amount and requested a refund along with the release of its bank guarantee. Defendants disagreed, claiming that plaintiff had failed to pay a substantial balance under the contract because it had received more tickets than it admitted and had not returned the unsold tickets. Consequently, they refused to release the bank guarantee.   Plaintiff's Claim: plaintiff claimed that government failed to provide all the tickets promised in the original tender under clause 2 of the contract, the payment should be reduced according to the reduced number of seats supplied, tickets used by the Nepal Police and the All Nepal Football Association should not be charged to plaintiff, after adjusting all payments plaintiff had already paid the required amount and had even overpaid. Therefore, the bank guarantee and other security should be released, and the excess payment should be refunded.   Defendants' Arguments: Defendants argued that plaintiff had received tickets worth more than it claimed plaintiff failed to return unsold tickets as required by the contract. A large balance amount remained unpaid. The plaintiff was therefore liable to pay the remaining amount. The Government was entitled to recover the unpaid amount from the bank guarantee and, if necessary, from the plaintiff's property. The suit was also argued to be filed beyond the limitation period.   Legal issues:
  1. Was the suit filed within the legal limitation period?
  2. Should the parties' rights and liabilities be determined according to the terms of the contract?
  3. Was plaintiff still liable to pay any remaining amount?
  4. Was plaintiff entitled to the release of the bank guarantee and security?
  Decisions of the Courts: Kathmandu District Court: Dismissed plaintiff's claim and held that plaintiff still had to pay the remaining contractual amount. It also refused to release the bank guarantee. The court found that plaintiff had not fully discharged its payment obligation under the contract.   Patan Appellate Court: Reversed the District Court's decision and ordered the release of plaintiff's bank guarantee. It held that under Clause 2 of the contract, the contract price had to be reduced because the Government supplied fewer tickets than agreed, and plaintiff had already paid the adjusted amount due.   Supreme Cout: Upheld the Appellate Court's decision and dismissed defendants' appeals. The Court held that the suit was filed within the limitation period and defendants failed to prove that any additional amount was payable, the contract terms were binding, and plaintiff had already fulfilled its payment obligation. Therefore, the release of the bank guarantee was proper.   Established Principles:
  1. Contract terms are binding like law upon the parties.
  2. If both parties continue to act under a contract even after the contractual period, the contract is treated as continuing until their obligations are settled.
  3. A cause of action arises only when there is a clear dispute requiring legal action.
  4. When the supplier fails to provide the agreed quantity under a contract, the other party cannot be compelled to pay for goods or services that were never supplied.
  5. A party claiming additional payment must objectively prove how much is actually payable.
  6. Security or a bank guarantee should be released once the contractual obligations have been fulfilled.
  Legal Doctrines: Sanctity of Contract: The parties must perform the contract according to the agreed terms, and those terms have the force of law between them. Cause of Action Doctrine: A lawsuit can be filed only after a legal cause of action has arisen. In this case, the cause of action arose when the Ministry formally demanded payment by letter. Burden of Proof: A party claiming additional money must prove, with objective evidence, how the amount is calculated.   Legal Maxims:
  1. Pacta sunt servanda: Agreements must be kept.
  2. Actio non datur non damnificato: No legal action arises until a legal injury or cause of action exists.
  3. Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat: The burden of proof lies on the person who asserts a fact.

title: Contract law Case: Krishna Bahadur Shrestha vs. Prachanda Shamsher, NKP (5t Semester)
content:
Contract law Case: Krishna Bahadur Shrestha vs. Prachanda Shamsher, NKP, 2025, N.4, P.80   Case: Transaction, Money Claim Plaintiff: Krishna Bahadur Shrestha Defendant: Prachanda Shamsher J.B.R Decision No: 405  

This case is related to money transaction deed.

  Facts of the case: Krishna Bahadur Shrestha, claimed that his grandmother Mohan Maya had been living under the care of defendant, Prachanda Shamsher J.B.R. Since there was no minor person in the household, plaintiff claimed that the gold and silver belonging to his grandmother were weighed and taken to the palace. The gold was stated to be 288 tola 8 masa and the silver 90 tola. According to plaintiff, the defendant had taken the property because it was required by the General Sahib and had made a written note regarding it. The grandmother gave that note to plaintiff near the end of her life in 2000 B.S, but plaintiff later lost it. Plaintiff further claimed that in 2003 B.S. his house was sold and Rs. 601/- also remained with defendant. The defendant had also arranged employment for him at Sundarijal. When plaintiff later requested payment, defendant allegedly replied through a letter dated 2010/01/15 BS that plaintiff's property had been used up and that the amount would be paid within one to one-and-a-half years after calculating the accounts. On the basis of this letter, the plaintiff claimed Rs. 47,388.90/-, representing the value of the gold, silver, diamonds and house amount, and requested that the amount be recovered from the defendant. Defendant denied the claim and stated that he had supported plaintiff when the he was an orphan. He claimed that he had provided plaintiff with rice and cash every month for some time. He denied having written the alleged note and argued that plaintiff had created a false and forged document because defendant had stopped providing such support. Defendant also denied the signature on the letter produced by plaintiff and alleged that it was forged and fabricated.   Plaintiff's claim: Plaintiff claimed that his grandmother's 288 tola 8 masa of gold and 90 tola of silver had been taken by defendant, Prachanda Shamsher J.B.R. He alleged that defendant had acknowledged responsibility through a written note and later through a letter dated 2010/01/15 BS, promising payment after calculation of the accounts. He also claimed Rs. 601/- from the sale of his house. Based on these claims, he sought recovery of Rs. 47,388.90/-.   Defendant's Argument: Defendant denied the claim and stated that he had previously supported plaintiff, who was an orphan, by providing rice and cash. He denied writing the alleged note and disputed the signature on the letter. He alleged that plaintiff had brought a false and forged claim after the financial support was stopped and therefore argued that plaintiff's claim should be dismissed.   Legal Issues:
  1. Can a letter be admitted as legal evidence for recovery of money when, even if the letter is genuine, it does not specify a definite amount payable and does not state how much money remains due?
  2. When a document is legally incapable of proving the claim, does the court need to decide whether it is genuine or forged?
  Decision of the courts: Kathmandu District: District Court rejected plaintiff's claim. The court compared defendant's genuine signatures with the signature on the disputed letter and found significant differences in the writing and signatures. Therefore, it held that the document was forged and could not support plaintiff's claim.   Appellate Court: Court upheld the decision of the original court. It agreed that the disputed document was not reliable and that plaintiff had failed to establish his claim for recovery of the amount.   Supreme Court Division Bench: It also agreed that the disputed document was forged after comparing it with defendant's genuine signatures in other official records. However, it found that the punishment imposed under the provision relating to jalsaji  was inappropriate and modified that part of the decision.   Judicial Committee: Judicial Committee agreed that the letter could not properly establish plaintiff's money claim. It observed that, even if the letter were genuine, the amount had to be determined from the terms actually stated in the letter rather than from plaintiff's total claim of Rs. 47,388.90/- It therefore recommended that the case be reviewed.   Supreme Court (Full Bench): Full Bench ultimately held that the letter could not be used to recover the claimed amount because it did not specify a definite amount payable or the amount remaining due. It could not therefore serve as a valid transaction or security document. Since the letter was legally insufficient to prove the claim even if genuine, Court held that there was no need to determine whether it was genuine or forged. Thus, the plaintiff's claim for recovery of money failed.     Established Principles:
  1. A definite amount is important in a money transaction document: Court held that the letter could not be treated as a proper security document because it did not fulfill the required legal conditions. It also could not be treated as a proper transaction document because there was no definite amount stated in the document.
  2. No need to decide genuine or forged when document is legally inadmissible: once the document was found incapable of being legally accepted as evidence for the money claim, it was unnecessary to decide whether the document was genuine or forged.
  3. Evidence must have legal relevance and effect: A document is not automatically useful evidence simply because it exists or contains some acknowledgment. It must have the legal capacity to establish the right claimed by the party relying upon it.

title: Contract Law Case: Kapilmuni vs. Deep Kumari, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Contract Law Case: Kapilmuni vs. Deep Kumari, NKP, 2020, P. 80   Case: Nasoo Dharaut (Deposit/Bailment) Plaintiff: Deep kumari Upadhyayani Defendant: Kapilmuni Upadhyay Decision Number: 195  

This case is related to deposit and bailment.

  Facts of the Case: Deep kumari Upadhyayani, stated that her husband had been imprisoned from Poush 2009 B.S. in connection with a case in Khotang. Since there was nobody knowledgeable at home and she feared theft or robbery, she entrusted property belonging to her, worth Rs. 1,722/- to defendant, Kapilmuni Upadhyaya, who was her relative and considered trustworthy. According to plaintiff, defendant agreed to return the property whenever she required it. A receipt/document dated 2010/11/17 B.S. was allegedly prepared in the handwriting of Krishna Prasad on behalf of defendant. When plaintiff's husband returned from prison in Ashadh 2011 B.S. plaintiff asked defendant to return the property. defendant allegedly replied that he had given the goods elsewhere and had spent the cash, and therefore could not return them. Plaintiff therefore asked court to order defendant either to return the same goods and cash or, if he could not return them, to pay their value of Rs. 1,722/-.   Plaintiff’s Claim: plaintiff claimed that she had entrusted property worth Rs. 1,722/- to defendant for safekeeping. A receipt dated 2010/11/17 BS had been prepared acknowledging the property. But defendant failed to return the property when demanded. Therefore, defendant should either return the property or pay its value of Rs. 1,722/-   Defendant’s Arguments: Defendant argued that if property worth Rs. 1,722/- had actually been deposited as naso dharaut, there should have been a legally proper document. The alleged document contained only one thumb impression and no witness. Krishna Prasad, who allegedly prepared the document, was the village jimwal and normally obtained thumb impressions from villagers on tax-payment receipts and argued that plaintiff might have obtained the thumb impression by deception or forgery also, plaintiff had no sufficient evidence proving that the property had actually been entrusted to him.   Legal Issues:
  1. Can a receipt relating to naso dharaut be legally recognized when it contains only one thumb impression instead of the required thumb impressions of both hands?
  2. Can a plaintiff succeed under the Naso Dharaut law when she cannot produce her witnesses to prove the transaction?
  3. Can an improperly executed document be used as sufficient evidence of the alleged deposit of property?
  Decisions of the Courts: Kavrepalanchok District Court: District Court rejected plaintiff's claim. Court found that the alleged Nasoo Dharaut document did not have legally required thumb impression and there was no proper witness to the document. Krishna Prasad, who allegedly wrote the document, did not appear before the court. Therefore, the document could not be treated as a valid legal document and court concluded that plaintiff had made a false claim based on a fraudulent document.   Appellate Court: It reversed the initial decision and ordered defendant to pay Rs. 1,722/- to plaintiff, Court relied particularly on examination of the thumb impression. Defendant's thumb impression on the alleged Nasoo Dharaut receipt was compared with his thumb impression on another document, and the evidence ultimately indicated that the impressions matched. The court also considered that defendant had not sufficiently proved his allegation that his thumb impression had been obtained through deception or fraud.   Supreme Court (Division Bench): The Division Bench affirmed the later appellate Court decision and held that defendant should pay Rs. 1,722/- One-thumb document was considered acceptable and fraud was not sufficiently proved, Defendant had not produced sufficient evidence to establish that he had been deceived into giving the thumb impression. Therefore, plaintiff's claim was considered proved.   Supreme Court Full Bench: The Full Bench reversed District Court's later decision and the Supreme Court Division Bench decision. The plaintiff's claim was held not proved, and the defendant was not required to pay Rs. 1,722/- Under the relevant provisions of the Kagad Janch (Document Examination) law, particularly Section 20 and Section 20(c), a document relating to Nasoo Dharaut required the thumb impressions of both hands. But the disputed document did not comply with this legal requirement. Therefore, the defective document could not be treated as sufficient proof of the alleged Nasoo Dharaut.   Established Principles:
  1. Statutory formalities must be followed: Where the law prescribes a specific form for a document, the parties must comply with that form.
  2. A defective document cannot by itself establish a legal claim: A document that does not satisfy mandatory legal requirements cannot automatically be accepted merely because it appears to acknowledge a transaction.
  3. Alternative oral evidence must actually be produced: Although Nasoo Dharaut 10 allowed a case to proceed on witness testimony where there was no written document in certain circumstances, the claimant still had to produce witnesses capable of proving the transaction.

title: Contract Law Case: Shiva Prasad & others vs. Institute of Sanskrit Studies Dang & others, NKP (5th Semester)
content:
Contract Law Case: Shiva Prasad & others vs. Institute of Sanskrit Studies Dang & others, NKP,2046, P. 7   Case: Bailment/Deposit Plaintiff: Institute of Sanskrit Studies Dang & others Defendants: Shiva prasad and others Decision No: 3688  

This case is related to Bailment and Deposit

 

Facts of the case: Defendants, including Shiv pd. Gautam, took approximately 500 bighas of land belonging to the educational institution on a five-year lease from 2030 to 2035 B.S. agreeing to pay Rs. 4,12,250/- as lease rent. During the lease arrangement, they received a 48-horsepower Belarus tractor, trailer, cultivator, disc/plough and toolbox for use with the leased land. They agreed to return the machinery in sound and working condition. On 2037/02/31 BS, they again gave a written undertaking to return the machinery in working condition by the end of Ashadh 2037. Defendants failed to return the machinery within the agreed period. Plaintiff therefore filed a case on 2039/02/30 BS, seeking either the return of the machinery in working condition or its value of Rs. 1,57,000/-, Defendants claimed that the tractor had been damaged by a flood in 2032 B.S. and remained in that condition. They argued that the loss resulted from a natural disaster and that they should therefore receive protection under Naso Dharaut (Bailment) No. 4.   Plaintiff's Claim: Plaintiff claimed that defendants had received the tractor and other machinery and they had agreed to return the machinery in sound and working condition but they failed to return it despite demands. They should either return the machinery in working condition or pay its value and claimed Rs. 1,57,000/- as the value of the machinery. Plaintiff also argued that defendants had not produced sufficient evidence proving that the machinery was damaged by the alleged flood.
